sources.text:
Poland deploys riot police, as court chief’s ousting sparks crisis
President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight, returning to Warsaw to deal with the turmoil at home
Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight, as riot police deployed around the country’s constitutional court on Friday following the suspension of its chief justice in a battle between the centrist government and the nationalist right.
Dozens of police guarded the entrance to the court as followers of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) protested against the ousting of constitutional court president Bogdan Swieczkowski.
The court’s official social media account said there had been a “coup d’etat” and some demonstrators chanted “Tusk traitor”, as they condemned the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Polish police deployed to top court after head judge suspended
Judge’s suspension is part of a long dispute over politicisation of the Constitutional Tribunal under former government.
Polish police have been deployed outside the country’s top court after demonstrators gathered to protest the suspension of its head judge.
Police said on Friday they entered the premises of the Constitutional Tribunal after incidents outside the court, including objects being thrown at police.
Protesters descended on the Warsaw court after it announced on Friday that its head, Bogdan Swieczkowski, had been suspended.
His suspension is related to a long-running dispute that has effectively paralysed the court.
Over the past six months, Swieczkowski used his power as head of the court to block judges elected by the current parliamentary majority from assuming their court duties.
Minister of Justice Waldemar Zurek told reporters on Friday that he had requested that Swieczkowski and his deputy’s immunity be lifted for failing to fulfil their duties by preventing judges from performing their work.
Swieczkowski was appointed to his position by Poland’s former nationalist Law and Justice party (PiS) government, which critics have accused of politicising the country’s courts.
Restoring the rule of law is the government’s duty, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on X following the news of Swieczkowski’s suspension.
“After years of lawlessness under PiS, this process is difficult, at times even painful, and requires decisive action. There is no other way,” said Tusk, leader of the Civic Coalition party.
News of Swieczkowski’s suspension brought crowds of PiS supporters to the gates of the Constitutional Tribunal. Police said they detained three people after some in the crowd launched “dangerous projectiles”.
Also on Friday, PiS-allied Polish President Karol Nawrocki announced he was turning his plane around while on the way to a sporting event in Senegal, saying: “At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland”.
Since his election in mid-2025, Nawrocki has refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by the Polish parliament.
Politicised judiciary
Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal has long been a point of serious political contention, with critics in Poland and across the European Union accusing PiS, which led the country from 2015 to 2023, of imposing political control over the court by electing judges friendly to the party and its policies.
When Poland’s pro-European government came to power, it promised to restore the independence of the judiciary. However, two attempts to do so have been vetoed by two PiS-aligned presidents – one of them Nawrocki.
Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the judges Nawrocki refused to swear in on the grounds of alleged flaws in her selection procedure, has now been placed in charge of the Constitutional Tribunal.
Politicians from PiS, currently Poland’s largest opposition force, have criticised Swieczkowski’s suspension.
“This is a blatant, criminal attack on the constitutional order,” former Justice Minister Zbigniew Ziobro wrote on X Friday.

sources.news_title: Tusk 'coup' as police invade top Polish court
sources.text:
Polish PM Donald Tusk has been accused of mounting a coup, after Polish police seized and occupied the country’s ‘Constitutional Tribunal’, Poland’s body that decides the application of its constitution.
In an X post this evening, 30 October 2026, Tusk blamed right-wing party PiS and claimed he had no other choice:
Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.
Constitutional war
A summary by Geoinsider explains what happened and why it matters:
- The Constitutional Tribunal’s leadership has been challenged.
Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska issued orders suspending Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański [Skwawkbox: both appointed by a PiS government] from their duties for one month. She claims authority to take over the Tribunal’s leadership as its most senior judge.
- Why did she do this?
Korwin-Piotrowska accuses the existing leadership of obstructing the work of judges elected by the current parliamentary majority, violating judicial procedures and preventing the proper functioning of the Tribunal. She also raised concerns about the court’s 2027 budget.
- The Tribunal rejects the orders.
Its existing leadership says the official website was illegally taken over and insists that Święczkowski remains president. The legality of Korwin-Piotrowska’s decisions is disputed.
- Police entered the building.
Following the announcement, demonstrators gathered outside the Tribunal. Tensions escalated, with some people reportedly climbing over the fence and throwing objects at police officers. Police intervened and several people were detained.
- Why is this Tribunal so important?
The Constitutional Tribunal determines whether laws and other legal acts comply with Poland’s Constitution. Its decisions can affect legislation, government actions and the country’s entire legal system. Control over its leadership therefore has major constitutional and political significance.
- This conflict has been building for months.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government and President Karol Nawrocki have been locked in a dispute over the Tribunal’s composition. Nawrocki refused to swear in three judges elected by parliament, while the Tribunal’s existing leadership refused to allow judges appointed by the current parliamentary majority to take their seats.
Tusk’s government does not recognise the Tribunal’s legitimacy and has refused to publish some of its rulings, citing controversial judicial appointments made under the previous PiS government.
- Political reactions are escalating.
PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński called on President Nawrocki to intervene, accusing Tusk’s government of turning Poland into a police state. Nawrocki cancelled his trip to Senegal and announced that he is returning to Poland.
Tusk, meanwhile, says restoring the rule of law is a difficult but necessary process.
The situation is still developing. Both sides dispute the legality of the actions taken, and the legal authority behind the latest orders remains unresolved.
Poland is now facing one of its most serious institutional confrontations in recent years. What happens next will depend on whether the two sides can resolve this dispute through legal and constitutional channels or whether the standoff escalates further. For now, Warsaw remains at the centre of a crisis that could have far-reaching consequences for the country’s institutions and political future.
Nawrocki has reportedly turned his flight to Senegal around and is returning to Poland. Tusk’s intervention may be linked to the EU’s determination to escalate its involvement in the Ukraine-Russia war. Poland’s constitution mandates who can declare war and under what circumstances. While it has no veto power, the court could potentially support a challenge to any declaration of war and PiS appointed judges might push for it to do so.

“At such a moment, the President must be in Poland,” Nawrocki wrote on X. “I’m interrupting my flight to Senegal. I’m returning.”
Police said they secured the tribunal after dozens of demonstrators gathered outside to protest what they described as the improper suspension of the court’s president by Poland’s pro-European government.
Authorities also reported that protesters threw dangerous objects at officers outside the building.
Some demonstrators outside the court prayed, while others displayed signs reading, “Tusk — a symbol of anti-Polish sentiment,” “Down with the commies and Tusk’s regime,” and “Stop destroying the state.”
Poland’s highest judicial institutions, including the Constitutional Tribunal, have become a central battleground between Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s pro-European government and the national-conservative Law and Justice party, or PiS. The party governed Poland from 2015 through 2023.
Critics have accused PiS of exerting political influence over key judicial bodies. Some of the party’s reforms prompted the European Union to impose financial penalties on Poland.
Nawrocki, who is allied with PiS, declined earlier this year to swear in three of the six judges chosen by parliament.

sources.news_title: Poland's top court claims ‘coup d’etat’ as riot police deployed and protests branded ‘very serious’ by Nigel Farage
sources.text:
Poland’s top court has accused Prime Minister Donald Tusk of launching a coup as riot police were deployed to and entered the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw amid clashes with protesters.
The constitutional crisis was triggered by the removal of Tribunal President Bogdan Swieczkowski while President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of Poland’s previous Eurosceptic Law and Justice (PiS) party government, was flying to Senegal. 
President Nawrocki has cut short his international visit and is currently racing back to Poland amid the standoff between the pro-EU Government of Mr Tusk and those connected to its PiS predecessors.
Polish Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek has demanded that the court strip Constitutional Tribunal President Święczkowski, who previously served as PiS deputy justice minister, and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution so that criminal charges can be brought. 
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," the Constitutional Tribunal said in a social media post.
“A coup d’état is underway in Poland,” MEP Arkadiusz Mularczyk wrote on X.
“The forces acting on behalf of the current government have unlawfully entered the Constitutional Tribunal and are preventing legally appointed judges from entering.”
Mr Tusk also addressed the chaos on social media, insisting that “restoring the rule of law is our duty”.
“After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.
“Either you will lead them out after a year of parliament, or they will lead us out of the European Union,” he added.
Reacting to the scenes, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: “The situation in Poland is very serious. Arrests and a raid on the constitutional court - all to defend the undemocratic EU.”
Earlier this year, President Nawrocki refused to swear in three judges appointed by parliament.
LATEST DEVELOPMENTS
Tribunal President Swieczkowski had also refused to allow judges elected by the current parliamentary majority to assume their duties.
The European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union had previously ruled that the PiS majority had improperly elected three judges.
They ruled that the top court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal".
Since then, Mr Tusk’s government has sought to undo PiS-government reforms using the EU’s ruling as a justification.
Outside the courthouse, police said objects had been hurled at officers by protesters.
The force said it had been deployed after receiving letters from the Prosecutor General and Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge on the tribunal, warning of threats to judges and staff.
PiS leader Jarsolaw Kaczynski joined protesters outside and attempted to force his way into the court building.
Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek blamed the Tribunal President for the chaos, accusing him of turning the constitutional court into his "private fiefdom", according to Politico.

Poland 'coup' latest: Riot police deployed in Warsaw as Donald Tusk issues warning
Cops have swarmed Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges
Riot police have been deployed at a court in Warsaw amid claims of a "coup d'etat".
An escalating row in Poland pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party.
The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański to be stripped of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and has defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw to protest. He warned: "After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court. "All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
Key Events
Judge bans entry to Constitutional Tribunal
Constitutional Tribunal Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska told the Polish Press Agency: "Out of concern for the life and health of people in and around the Constitutional Tribunal, I do not consent to anyone entering the premises of the Constitutional Tribunal.
"We can meet with the President of the Republic of Poland at the Presidential Palace."
She has also issued a statement in which she emphasised that MPs and senators cannot perform any activities on the premises of the Constitutional Tribunal.
Ambassador of the Republic of Poland in China resigns
Ambassador of the Republic of Poland in China, Jakub Kumoch, has resigned.
In a post on X, he said: "In light of the events in the country, I have concluded that it is no longer possible for me to continue serving as the Ambassador of the Republic of Poland.
"As of today, I have submitted my resignation and a request for recall."
Radosław Sikorski, Polish deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, called Mr Kumoch's decision "unprofessional".
He replied to Mr Kumoch's post: "I acknowledge the unprofessional conclusion of your mission. You no longer represent the Republic."
President meets Święczkowski
Just before 11pm local time, Polish president Karol Nawrocki was seen arriving at the Presidential Palace following his trip to Senegal, which he had to cut short.
He is understood to have now met with the First President of the Supreme Court, Zbigniew Kapiński, and with Bogdan Święczkowski.
'The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse'
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose has described tonight's events at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal as "very serious".
Mr Rose added that the thousands gathered outside the tribunal make an "already dangerous situation more combustible".
He said: "We appear to be witnessing an unprecedented confrontation over the government’s use of state power and the independence and authority of a constitutional institution.
"Both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why. Whatever the facts ultimately establish, thousands gathering outside the Tribunal make an already dangerous situation more combustible.
"The last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse. America is on Poland’s side.
"It is not our place to judge or interfere in its internal affairs. Our concern is for the stability, security, and democratic future of a country we are proud to call our friend and ally."
Święczkowski tried to get into tribunal as protesters cut fence chain
At around 8pm local time, Bogdan Święczkowski arrived at the Constitutional Tribunal and tried to convince the police to let him into the Constitutional Tribunal, TVN24 reports.
A chain that was blocking a fence was cut by protesters and Święczkowski reportedly entered the gate but stopped before the police cordon.
A few minutes later, he announced his withdrawal, the Polish news outlet adds.
Święczkowski reportedly said he is the "sole administrator of the Constitutional Tribunal building" as the president of the Constitutional Tribunal.
"Remember, the Tribunal is made up of people and judges," he told those gathered in front of the Constitutional Tribunal, announcing that "all legal judges" would arrive on Saturday and demand entry to the building.
Member of the European Parliament Arkadiusz Mularczyk said: "A coup d’état is underway in Poland.
"The forces acting on behalf of the current government have unlawfully entered the Constitutional Tribunal and are preventing legally appointed judges from entering."
'Threats to life and health' of judges
Warsaw Police said in a statement released this evening that the chief of the national police in Poland was informed in a letter that "planned activities" on the premises of the Constitutional Tribunal could create "threats to the life and health of judges and employees".
The letter also described the possibility of a "risk of disruption to public order".
The statement read: "We reiterate that the Police are not conducting any actions within the seat of the Tribunal, limiting them exclusively to the external area.
"The officers' actions are aimed at fulfilling statutory duties, in particular the legal obligation to ensure public safety and order.
"They do not constitute interference in the activities of the Constitutional Tribunal as an institution."
Who is Bogdan Święczkowski?
Information about the suspension of the president of the Constitutional Tribunal, Bogdan Święczkowski, was published on the court's website around 6pm local time. The Tribunal's website went down soon after.
Święczkowski became head of the Constitutional Tribunal under the PiS government, and Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal.
Politicians from PiS, currently the largest opposition force, have criticised Święczkowski’s suspension.
Three people arrested
Three people have been arrested after allegedly jumping the fence and entering the Constitutional Tribunal grounds, according to Warsaw police.
The force said: "Procedural proceedings against those detained will be conducted pursuant to Article 193 of the Penal Code.
"Officers are conducting operations aimed at restoring public order and safety on Aleja Szucha in front of the Constitutional Tribunal headquarters. Dangerous objects were thrown at the officers."
Polish president cuts Senegal trip short
Polish President Karol Nawrocki, who was flying to Senegal, said he turned his flight back because of the situation.
"At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland. I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," he wrote on X.
The president had left earlier today and was scheduled to attend events related to the 4th Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar tomorrow.

Polish president Karol Nawrocki turned back his plane en route to Senegal on Friday as the country’s top court was thrown into chaos after its president was suspended.
Police and protesters clashed outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw after the government suspended its two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them. A long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution.
Earlier this year, Mr Nawrocki, an ally of Poland's former nationalist government of the Law and Justice or PiS party, refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, who was a deputy justice minister under PiS, declined to allow judges elected by the current parliamentary majority to assume their duties.

sources.text: Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight as riot police deployed around the country’s constitutional court Friday following the suspension of its chief justice in a battle between the centrist government and the nationalist right. Dozens of police guarded the entrance to the court as followers of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) protested the ousting of constitutional court president Bogdan Swieczkowski. The court’s official X social media account said there had been a “coup d’etat” and some demonstrators chanted “Tusk traitor” as they condemned the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Some tried to force their way through security barricades. Police said they had arrested three people who had tried to enter the court complex. Tusk was “trampling on our constitutional rights”, demonstrator Tomasz Zaleski told AFP outside the court. Tusk’s government has been trying for weeks to force out the court’s judges, who were appointed by the previous PiS government that ruled from 2015 to 2023. The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over European Union law and the EU accused Poland’s highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time. Mid-flight chaos Tusk, a strongly pro-EU figure, vowed to end the dispute with Brussels after winning an election in 2023. But the country’s president, a right wing independent, has blocked his nominations to the court. Former PiS prime minister Jaroslaw Kaczysnki addressed the demonstration and called for Nawrocki to act. The president said he had called off an official trip to Senegal in mid-flight and ordered it back to Warsaw. Back in the capital, Nawrocki held a meeting with Swieczkowski and the court’s first chief justice Zbigniew Kapinski at the presidential palace. No details were given of any possible action. The suspension of Swieczkowski was announced by another judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska who said the move was needed to restore the rule of law. Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek, who is also the attorney general, told journalists he had requested the lifting of the legal immunity of Swieczkowski and his deputy Bartlomiej Sochanski. “This court has become private property; we must restore its proper functioning,” he added. Tusk justified the action in a comment on the X platform. “Restoring the rule of law is our duty,” he said. “After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” The constitutional court’s official website was not accessible on Friday evening. Its X account said there had been a “coup d’etat” and that Swieczkowski remained in office. Korwin-Piotrowska could not become interim chief as she had not been sworn in by the president, it added. Amid the confusion, Korwin-Piotrowska commented: “In modern Europe, a democratic state cannot function without a constitutional court (...) that acts as a guarantor of citizens’ rights and freedoms.” Gaël Branchereau and Bernard Osser, AFP

This is a breaking news story and may be updated as it develops.
Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) was plunged into chaos on Friday evening as one group of judges, backed by the government, moved to take control of the court from its chief justice, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and President Karol Nawrocki.
One of the government-backed judges said that she had suspended the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, from his duties. Police have surrounded the court and were seen preventing Święczkowski from entering the grounds after his supporters had cut through the fence with a power tool.
Święczkowski and the opposition claim that an illegal “coup d’etat” is underway. Nawrocki, who had been flying to Senegal for a state visit, ordered his plane to turn around and return to Warsaw.

— Jan Molski 🇵🇱 (@JanMolski) October 30, 2026
The dramatic events follow a years-long crisis around the TK. Since the current government – a coalition ranging from left to centre right led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk – came to power in 2023, it has refused to recognise the court’s legitimacy.
That is because three of its judges were unlawfully appointed under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, which was widely seen to have brought the court under political control.
As a result, Tusk’s government has ignored the TK’s rulings and, until this year, refused to even nominate new judges to fill vacancies that arose on the court’s 15-person bench.
‘
That changed in March, when the ruling coalition began filling the backlog of empty seats. So far this year, parliament has chosen eight new judges, meaning that its nominees in theory now have a majority on the court.
However, under Polish law, although new TK judges are chosen by parliament, they must swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki, who is aligned with PiS, has refused to swear in five of those eight new judges, citing concerns over how they were chosen or their qualifications.
Those five judges arranged their own swearing-in ceremonies in parliament and submitted their oaths to the president’s office. However, Święczkowski, who before being appointed as a TK judge had served in the former PiS government, refused to accept those five judges on the court.
In doing so, he ignored an order by the European Court of Human Rights that the judges be allowed to take up their positions. Święczkowski argued that the ECHR had no authority to issue such a ruling.
The standoff between the government and president over Poland’s constitutional court deepened today, as Maciej Berek, whom the prime minister recently described as his “right-hand man”, took his oath as a new judge without the presence of the president https://t.co/MrExiJRsEN
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 14, 2026
Rumours have long swirled that the government would introduce those judges onto the court by force. PiS supporters have been camped outside the TK grounds for weeks with the aim of preventing that from happening.
On Friday evening, large numbers of riot police were deployed around the TK. On the court’s website, a brief statement appeared, saying that a “break in the activities” of Święczkowski and his deputy chief justice, Bartłomiej Sochański, had been ordered.
The statement did not say who had ordered that break, but it cited article 130 of the law on common courts, under which the president of a court or the justice minister can order an immediate break in a judge’s official duties if they are caught in the act of committing an offence.
However, Marcin Matczak, a prominent scholar of constitutional law who was also a critic of PiS’ judicial reforms, wrote on social media, that, while the justice minister exercises oversight over common courts, he cannot do so over the TK.
“I consider Bogdan Święczkowski to be the worst person to serve as the president of the TK,” wrote Matczak. “I never thought I’d end up defending him, but this legal basis [for suspending Święczkowski] is nonexistent for a million reasons.”

Meanwhile, Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, issued a statement announcing that he had submitted motions to the TK to waive the immunity from prosecution of Świeczkowski and Sochański.
He said that the documents had been “delivered to the longest-serving judge of the Constitutional Tribunal”.
That was a reference to Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, one of the TK judges whom Nawrocki has refused to swear in. She told state broadcaster TVP that it was she who had issued the order to suspend Święczkowski from his duties.
She justified her action by accusing Święczkowski of blocking judges from taking up their positions and of overseeing irregularities in the assignment of judges to cases, reports Polskie Radio.
Korwin-Piotrowska’s claim to have the longest tenure among TK judges relates not to her service on tribunal itself, but to the fact that she first began her judicial career in 1995.

Polands President cuts short Senegal visit as police cordon off top court after chiefs suspension in clash with PM Tusk - The Tribune
sources.text:
Poland's President cuts short Senegal visit as police cordon off top court after chief's suspension in clash with PM Tusk
Warsaw [Poland], October 31 (ANI): Poland has plunged into a severe constitutional and political crisis following an intense escalation of the ongoing power struggle between Prime Minister Donald Tusk and President Karol Nawrocki, after heavily armed police units cordoned off the headquarters of the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw on Friday night.
A de facto confrontation has erupted within a principal state institution, leaving the final outcome of the standoff uncertain. Law enforcement officers surrounded the premises of the Tribunal in substantial numbers, though they did not physically enter the building.
The deployment of police was requested by Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, who pointed to a potential risk to the safety of judges and administrative personnel.
The crisis intensified rapidly after Korwin-Piotrowska issued a one-month suspension against Constitutional Tribunal President Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, thereby temporarily assuming control of the institution.
According to bulletins issued by Poland's official news agency PAP, the suspensions stemmed from accusations that the two senior figures had improperly discharged their official duties and blocked legally appointed magistrates, including Korwin-Piotrowska, from taking part in the Tribunal's proceedings.
The official profiles of the suspended figures subsequently vanished from the court's online portal. In response, the Constitutional Tribunal issued a statement via social media asserting that its website had suffered an "illegal takeover". It argued that Korwin-Piotrowska lacked the authority to speak for the court and cautioned that those involved were "committing the crime of coup d'état".
Tensions surrounding the institution have built steadily since early 2026, sparked when President Nawrocki declined to administer oaths to three out of six magistrates selected by Parliament. The broader dispute originates from fundamental disagreements regarding the Tribunal's membership. The administration headed by Prime Minister Tusk refuses to acknowledge the validity of rulings issued by judges appointed during the preceding Law and Justice (PiS) administration.
Conversely, President Nawrocki and Święczkowski have declined to recognise magistrates chosen by the Sejm in 2026.
Judge Korwin-Piotrowska remains central to this friction, as President Nawrocki previously rejected her oath of office while Święczkowski blocked her participation in hearings. This ongoing political jockeying between the governing Civic Platform (PO) and the former PiS administration has fuelled years of controversy surrounding the court's legitimacy.
Defending his administration's position, Prime Minister Tusk insisted that reviving the rule of law remains paramount following years of friction under the previous PiS leadership.
"Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way," Tusk wrote on X.
The rapidly deteriorating situation forced President Nawrocki to cut short an official mission to Senegal and journey back to Poland. "At such a moment, the President must be in Poland. I'm interrupting my flight to Senegal. I'm returning," Nawrocki wrote on X. Upon landing, the President is scheduled to hold consultations with Supreme Court President Kapiński regarding the attempted suspension of the Constitutional Tribunal President, according to his Chief of Staff.
Meanwhile, Poland's Ambassador to China, Jakub Kumoch, tendered his resignation on Friday evening, declaring that "in light of the events in the country", it was "no longer possible" for him to maintain his diplomatic post.
PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński censured the Tusk administration, accusing the government of utilising state apparatuses to target the Constitutional Tribunal and warning that the nation was sliding towards authoritarianism.
"From today, Poland becomes a police state, and from there there is already a direct path to authoritarianism, and then to totalitarianism," he stated.
"The Tribunal is the guarantee of our freedom and sovereignty. Tusk's trampling of the law knows no limits," Kaczyński added.
Similar condemnation came from European Parliament members associated with Nawrocki's Law and Justice party. MEP Arkadiusz Mularczyk characterised the developments as a coup d'état, claiming that agents acting on behalf of the incumbent executive had unlawfully forced entry into the Constitutional Tribunal to bar accredited judges from the premises.
Former Polish prime minister and MEP Beata Szydło also condemned the security operation on social media. "Shocking scenes in Poland. Police, dispatched by the Tusk government, have forced their way into the independent Constitutional Tribunal," she wrote on X.
She further claimed that security details protecting the building and judicial records were dismissed, while the court's vice-president was barred from entering.
This latest confrontation marks a dramatic escalation in Poland's protracted institutional deadlock, with rival factions maintaining starkly conflicting viewpoints concerning the government's intervention and the legal standing of the Tribunal's leadership. (ANI)

sources.text:
Police deployed during stand-off over control of top Poland court
Riot police have been deployed at Poland's Constitutional Court amid an escalating stand-off between the government and the court's top judges.
The row pits the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk against his predecessors from the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS).
The police intervention came after Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek said he had requested stripping the court's President Bogdan Święczkowski and Vice-President Bartłomiej Sochański of their immunity from prosecution to bring criminal charges against them.
Tusk has vowed to depoliticise the judiciary, and on Friday defended the move as PiS supporters gathered outside the court premises in Warsaw in protest.
Riot police were deployed to prevent any demonstrators from entering the court building.
In a social media post, the Constitutional Court wrote that the two judges the government wants to prosecute were still the legally appointed senior justices of the court.
"All persons participating in these actions are committing the crime of a coup d'etat," it said.
In a social media post, Tusk wrote: "Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of Law and Justice's lawlessness, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way."
President Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by PiS, ordered his plane be turned back to Warsaw on his way to Senegal to attend the Summer Youth Olympic Games.
The PiS-led government took office in 2015 and moved swiftly to appoint judges to the court to gain a majority there because the court has the power to decide on the legality of legislation.
Leading European courts - the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Justice of the European Union - subsequently ruled the PiS majority had elected three of the judges improperly because they were duplicating positions that had been validly filled by the previous parliament.
The European courts ruled Poland's Constitutional Court was no longer an "independent and impartial tribunal", and Tusk's government has used those rulings as a basis to stop publishing the tribunal's rulings.
Tusk has failed to undo the PiS-era changes, partially because Nawrocki and his PiS-backed predecessor Andrzej Duda used their presidential vetoes to block his attempts.
Nawrocki has also refused to swear in five Constitutional Court judges elected by parliament since March on the grounds of alleged flaws in their selection procedure.
One of those judges, Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.
Earlier this month, the Council of Europe's advisory body on constitutional matters, the Venice Commission, said Nawrocki should swear-in the judges to allow them to sit on the court's bench.
Justice Minister Żurek said Święczkowski and his vice-president should face criminal charges for not allowing the judges to adjudicate.
Some of Tusk's supporters have accused him of failing to act decisively to reverse the PiS-era reforms.
Parliamentary elections are scheduled next year, and some see his move as an attempt to boost Tusk's popularity among those voters.
But his actions have been criticised. In September, Tusk put forward a politician, Maciej Berek, a lawyer who served as a minister in his cabinet, as a judge candidate to the court.
Lawyer Marcin Matczak, a critic of the PiS-era judicial reform who has stated he considers Święczkowski to be the court's worst president, said his suspension had no legal basis "for a million reasons".
"Today's action at the Constitutional Court, in my opinion, buries this body and the issue of the rule of law for two decades," Prof Matczak wrote on social media.
"Images of armed police and legal interpretations according to which the minister of justice can remove the president of the Constitutional Court by decree will have a powerful, anti-rule of law backlash for years to come," he added.

Polish riot police deployed as deposed court chief sets off crisis
Warsaw (AFP) – Poland's President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight as riot police deployed around the country's constitutional court Friday following the suspension of its chief justice in a battle between the centrist government and the nationalist right.
Issued on: Modified:
Dozens of police guarded the entrance to the court as followers of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) protested the ousting of constitutional court president Bogdan Swieczkowski.
The court's official X social media account said there had been a "coup d'etat" and some demonstrators chanted "Tusk traitor" as they condemned the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
Some tried to force their way through security barricades. Police said they had arrested three people who had tried to enter the court complex.
Tusk was "trampling on our constitutional rights", demonstrator Tomasz Zaleski told AFP outside the court.
Tusk's government has been trying for weeks to force out the court's judges, who were appointed by the previous PiS government that ruled from 2015 to 2023.
The court frequently ruled in favour of Polish legislation over European Union law and the EU accused Poland's highest court of being too close to the nationalist political power of the time.
Mid-flight chaos
Tusk, a strongly pro-EU figure, vowed to end the dispute with Brussels after winning an election in 2023. But the country's president, a right wing independent, has blocked his nominations to the court.
Former PiS prime minister Jaroslaw Kaczysnki addressed the demonstration and called for Nawrocki to act. The president said he had called off an official trip to Senegal in mid-flight and ordered it back to Warsaw.
Back in the capital, Nawrocki held a meeting with Swieczkowski and the court's first chief justice Zbigniew Kapinski at the presidential palace. No details were given of any possible action.
The suspension of Swieczkowski was announced by another judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska who said the move was needed to restore the rule of law.
Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek, who is also the attorney general, told journalists he had requested the lifting of the legal immunity of Swieczkowski and his deputy Bartlomiej Sochanski.
"This court has become private property; we must restore its proper functioning," he added.
Tusk justified the action in a comment on the X platform.
"Restoring the rule of law is our duty," he said.
"After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way."
The constitutional court's official website was not accessible on Friday evening.
Its X account said there had been a "coup d'etat" and that Swieczkowski remained in office.
Korwin-Piotrowska could not become interim chief as she had not been sworn in by the president, it added.
Amid the confusion, Korwin-Piotrowska commented: "In modern Europe, a democratic state cannot function without a constitutional court (...) that acts as a guarantor of citizens' rights and freedoms."

sources.news_title: Polish President Aborts Senegal Trip as Police Enter Constitutional Tribunal Grounds Amid Leadership Dispute
sources.text:
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom
WARSAW, Poland — Polish President Karol Nawrocki abruptly turned his aircraft around Friday, Oct. 30, abandoning a diplomatic trip to Senegal after police entered the grounds of the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw and the court announced the suspension of its president, Bogdan Święczkowski.
The confrontation intensified an ongoing dispute between Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s governing coalition and Poland’s conservative opposition over control of the country’s constitutional court, with opposition leaders accusing the government of attempting to take over the judiciary.
Police arrived at the tribunal’s headquarters on Szucha Avenue during the late afternoon. Video footage circulating on X showed officers at the premises as demonstrators and opposition politicians gathered outside.
The Warsaw Metropolitan Police confirmed that officers were operating on the tribunal’s grounds but disputed claims that they had forcibly entered the court building or removed its security personnel.
Police said the deployment followed information from Constitutional Tribunal Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska warning of possible threats to judges and court employees, as well as disturbances to public order. Authorities also reported that objects had been thrown at officers during confrontations outside the building.
According to Reuters, the tribunal announced Święczkowski’s suspension on its website as the police operation unfolded.
Polish media subsequently reported that Deputy Tribunal President Bartłomiej Sochański had also been suspended from his duties for one month, pending disciplinary proceedings. Korwin-Piotrowska was reported to have assumed responsibility for the court’s leadership, although the legal basis and validity of the changes remained disputed.
The developments prompted Nawrocki to terminate his flight to Senegal, where he had been traveling for an official visit.
“At such a moment, the President must be in Poland. I’m interrupting my flight to Senegal. I’m returning,” Nawrocki announced on X.
The president’s office subsequently confirmed that he had ordered his aircraft to return because of developments at the Constitutional Tribunal.
Tusk defended his government’s approach to the judiciary, arguing that decisive measures were necessary to reverse changes introduced during the previous Law and Justice government.
“Restoring the rule of law is our duty. After years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way,” Tusk wrote on X.
The prime minister’s remarks reflected his administration’s longstanding position that judicial reforms enacted during Law and Justice’s years in power undermined judicial independence and violated constitutional principles.
Law and Justice, known by its Polish abbreviation PiS, governed Poland from 2015 until 2023. Its changes to judicial appointments and disciplinary procedures generated prolonged disputes with European Union institutions, which accused the government of weakening judicial independence.
Tusk’s government, which assumed office in December 2023, pledged to reverse those measures. Its efforts have encountered resistance from judges appointed under the previous administration and from presidents aligned with the conservative opposition.
Friday’s confrontation concerned the Constitutional Tribunal, which adjudicates disputes involving the Polish Constitution and the validity of legislation.
Święczkowski, a former national prosecutor associated with the previous PiS administration, has resisted attempts by the current parliamentary majority to reorganize the tribunal’s membership.
Earlier in 2026, Nawrocki refused to administer the oath of office to three of six judges selected by parliament. Święczkowski subsequently declined to allow judges chosen by the governing majority to assume their duties.
The resulting disagreements have significantly restricted the tribunal’s ability to function.
Tusk’s governing coalition maintains that the existing judicial leadership has perpetuated institutional problems inherited from the previous government. Opposition politicians argue that the coalition is attempting to bypass constitutional procedures to install judges more favorable to its policies.
Law and Justice leader Jarosław Kaczyński denounced Friday’s police operation, accusing the government of using law enforcement to take control of the tribunal.
In a statement posted on X, Kaczyński described the developments as an attack on the Constitutional Tribunal and claimed Poland was “becoming a police state.”
He urged citizens to continue demonstrating and called on Nawrocki to exercise his constitutional powers to challenge the government’s actions.
Kaczyński also appeared outside the tribunal’s headquarters, where opposition lawmakers and demonstrators had assembled.
According to Polish broadcaster Onet, he appealed directly to Nawrocki to intervene within the limits of the presidency’s constitutional authority.
Other opposition figures characterized the operation in similarly severe terms.
Polish member of the European Parliament Grzegorz Braun, a nationalist politician who has repeatedly criticized the European Union, compared the developments to Poland’s May 1926 coup, when Józef Piłsudski seized power after several days of fighting.
Braun also called for Poland to withdraw from the European Union.
His historical comparison and allegations of a coup reflected his political interpretation of the confrontation; no independent judicial finding had established that Friday’s events constituted a coup or an unlawful government takeover.
Polish police maintained that their actions were limited to protecting personnel and restoring public order.
The Warsaw Metropolitan Police said officers were acting under statutory powers after receiving information about potential threats to the safety of judges and employees.
The police statement also emphasized that officers were respecting the tribunal’s institutional independence and were not intervening in its judicial functions.
Reports about the precise location and actions of police officers differed throughout the evening. Some media outlets reported that officers had entered the building, while police maintained that their personnel were operating on the grounds rather than inside the court itself.
The Associated Press reported that demonstrators breached a fence outside the tribunal and threw objects at officers, resulting in three arrests.
The tribunal’s website briefly displayed an announcement concerning the suspension of its leadership before becoming unavailable. That disruption prevented independent confirmation of all details surrounding the purported disciplinary action.
The circumstances under which the leadership change was announced, and whether it complied with applicable Polish constitutional and judicial procedures, remained unresolved Friday evening.
Poland’s president and prime minister occupy separate constitutional roles. The president serves as head of state and possesses certain appointment and veto powers, while the prime minister leads the government and directs its executive administration.
Nawrocki’s opposition to the governing coalition’s judicial restructuring has created repeated institutional confrontations, particularly over judicial appointments and the authority of courts established or reorganized during the previous PiS administration.
The Constitutional Tribunal dispute has also attracted scrutiny from European institutions because judicial independence and the effectiveness of constitutional review have been longstanding points of disagreement between Warsaw and Brussels.
Tusk’s government argues that its measures are intended to restore judicial independence and compliance with constitutional standards. Opposition leaders contend that the methods being used threaten the separation of powers.
Friday’s suspension announcement, police deployment and interruption of Nawrocki’s international trip brought those competing claims into direct confrontation.
By Friday evening, the status of the tribunal’s leadership remained disputed, with no final judicial resolution establishing the legality of the suspensions or the reported transfer of authority.
Nawrocki’s return to Warsaw placed the presidency at the center of the confrontation as the government and opposition continued disputing control of one of Poland’s principal constitutional institutions.

PiS supporters gathered outside the court, chanting "Tusk traitor", according to an AFP journalist at the scene. Some demonstrators also held rosaries and religious images while praying.
Why did the president cancel his Africa visit
Nawrocki, an independent politician aligned with the right, cancelled his planned flight to Senegal for an official visit and decided to return to Warsaw as the confrontation escalated.
His decision came as police presence increased around the Constitutional Tribunal and opposition supporters mobilised against the suspension of its chief justice.
What is the court's position
The constitutional tribunal's official X account rejected the suspension, calling it a "coup d'etat" and maintaining that Swieczkowski continued to hold the post.
It also argued that Korwin-Piotrowska could not take over as interim chief justice because she had not been sworn in by the president. The court's official website was inaccessible on Friday evening.

Protesters gathered outside the court building, denouncing what they described as an attack on the tribunal by Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

“We are deeply saddened that Donald Tusk is taking us back several decades, reducing us to a second-class country,” said Patryk Jaki, a PiS member of the European Parliament.
“Why is Donald Tusk doing this? His main reason is the Constitutional Tribunal’s ruling that Polish law takes precedence over European law,” he added, according to Onet.
According to the Polish Press Agency (PAP), Swieczkowski entered the tribunal’s grounds after his supporters cut through a gate lock with a circular saw. He subsequently left the grounds and called for calm.
Police, meanwhile, established an additional security cordon outside the courthouse. Three people were detained for climbing over the fence.

Police said they had deployed officers following requests from the prosecutor general and Korwin-Piotrowska. The requests cited possible threats to judges and staff and the risk of public disorder. Police denied entering the court building, saying their operations were confined to its grounds and surrounding public areas.
Tusk defended what he described as efforts to restore the rule of law following the previous government led by the conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. “After years of lawlessness under PiS, this is a difficult, sometimes painful process that requires decisive action. There is no other way,” he wrote on X.
President Karol Nawrocki cut short a planned trip to Senegal and turned his plane around to return to Poland amid the escalating crisis.
After landing in Warsaw, Nawrocki held an emergency meeting with Zbigniew Kapinski, the head of Poland’s Supreme Court. His office said he would also meet with Swieczkowski. The Constitutional Tribunal rules on whether laws comply with the Constitution, while the Supreme Court reviews lower court decisions and oversees the ordinary judicial system.
The tribunal remains dominated by judges appointed by PiS before Tusk took power in 2023. Tusk has been locked in a prolonged battle with Nawrocki and PiS over judicial appointments. Nawrocki has refused to administer the oath to five judges elected by parliament, while the tribunal’s existing leadership has challenged their authority to take up their posts.
During PiS’s eight years in power, the EU repeatedly criticized the party’s judicial reforms, accusing it of undermining judicial independence. PiS defended the reforms as necessary to strengthen Poland’s sovereignty and accused Brussels of interfering in the country’s internal affairs.
In recent months, Nawrocki has also taken a more confrontational stance toward Ukraine, demanding that Kiev stop honoring nationalist paramilitaries who collaborated with Nazi Germany during the early stages of its invasion of the Soviet Union and participated in massacres of Polish civilians in what is now western Ukraine. Tusk has adopted a more conciliatory approach, emphasizing the importance of continued support for Ukraine in its conflict with Russia.
Shortly after midnight on Saturday, US Ambassador Tom Rose issued a cautiously worded statement, noting that “both sides offer sharply different accounts of what happened and why.” He urged all parties to avoid violence, warning that “the last thing Poland needs is a confrontation that spirals into something far worse.”

sources.news_title: Polish President aircraft bound for Dakar is returning due to current situation around the Constitutional Tribunal
sources.text:
WARSAW — Two Polish government aircraft bound for Dakar have aborted their journey and are returning to Warsaw following escalations surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal, officials confirmed on Friday.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki announced he was interrupting his working visit to Senegal to return to Poland immediately after reports surfaced regarding police presence on the premises of the Constitutional Tribunal.
“At a time like this, the President must be in Poland. I’m canceling my flight to Senegal. I’m returning.”
While police officers have been deployed to the Tribunal’s grounds, authorities clarified that officers remain outside and have not entered the building itself.
The two presidential Boeing 737-800 aircraft originally departed Warsaw Chopin Airport (WAW) at 14:45 CET. President Nawrocki was en route to the Republic of Senegal for an official visit centered on preparations for the 4th Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar.
Both aircraft redirected mid-flight and are scheduled to land back at Warsaw Chopin Airport by 21:30 CET. Further updates regarding the situation at the Constitutional Tribunal and official statements from the presidential administration are expected following President Nawrocki’s arrival.
